justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, likely somewhere around 305–308 for the underlying asset (which based on the numbers appears consistent with something like the S&P 500 ETF SPY, a mid-cap index, or a similar equity instrument trading in that range). For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price with only a slight upward nudge, reflecting mean-reversion tendencies and the absence of any strong directional catalyst in the immediate term. For the one-week and one-month horizons, I applied a small positive drift consistent with the long-run equity risk premium, while acknowledging that over those timeframes, macro and sentiment factors become increasingly relevant. The gradual step-up from 307.5 to 308.0 to 310.0 is intentionally conservative — it reflects baseline upward bias without overconfidence in any particular directional move.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. Daily price moves in equity indices or ETFs in this price range are commonly 0.5–1.5%, which supports a roughly ±7 range for the one-day 90% CI. As the horizon extends to a week, uncertainty compounds, and I widened the interval to roughly ±13 points to capture the broader distribution of weekly returns. For the one-month window, I used a still wider ±27-point range, reflecting that a full month introduces earnings cycles, Fed communications, geopolitical developments, and shifts in investor positioning that are genuinely hard to anticipate.

The main risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals fall into two categories: sharp downside shocks and strong momentum-driven rallies. On the downside, unexpected macroeconomic data (a surprise inflation print, weak employment numbers, or a credit event) could trigger a risk-off move exceeding 5–10% within days, which would breach the lower bound of even the one-month interval. A geopolitical escalation or financial contagion event could similarly cause a fast, large drawdown. On the upside, a dovish policy pivot, a strong earnings season, or a short-squeeze dynamic in a risk-on environment could push prices well above 337 within a month.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry meaningful model uncertainty on top of the stated statistical uncertainty. I don't have access to real-time market data, order flow, or options-implied volatility surfaces, all of which a professional forecaster would use to sharpen these intervals.
